title: The Attached Pronouns (Al-Ḍamāʾir al-Muttaṣilah)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 9; Ryding Ch. 12)
objectives: Attach pronominal suffixes to nouns to express possession (functioning as muḍāf ilayh).
Attach pronominal suffixes to prepositions (e.g., لَهُ, مِنْهُ, فِيهِ).
Apply the vowel-harmony shift in 3rd-person suffixes (-hu / -hum → -hi / -him) after kasrah or yāʾ.
recallPrompt: From Chapter 8: Why does a noun lose the definite article (الـ) and tanwīn when it serves as muḍāf?

sections.heading: Enclitic Pronouns on Nouns and Prepositions
sections.body: Arabic uses attached pronominal suffixes (al-ḍamāʾir al-muttaṣilah) rather than separate possessive adjectives ('my', 'his', 'their'). Attached to a noun, the suffix acts as the muḍāf ilayh—so the noun drops the definite article (الـ) and tanwīn. Attached to a preposition, the suffix serves as its genitive object.

sections.label: 3rd-Person Vowel Harmony
sections.summary: The 3rd-person suffixes ـهُ, ـهُمَا, ـهُمْ, ـهُنَّ shift their ḍammah to kasrah (ـهِ, ـهِمَا, ـهِمْ, ـهِنَّ) whenever immediately preceded by a kasrah (-i) or a yāʾ (يْ / ـِي).

sections.translation: In his house are many books.
sections.irab: فِي: حَرْفُ جَرٍّ | بَيْتِ: اسْمٌ مَجْرُورٌ وَهُوَ مُضَافٌ | ـهِ: ضَمِيرٌ مُتَّصِلٌ فِي مَحَلِّ جَرٍّ مُضَافٌ إِلَيْهِ
sections.notes: بَيْتِ is genitive after فِي, so the attached pronoun ـهُ shifts to ـهِ (baytihi).

sections.heading: 1st-Person Singular (ـِي) Overrides Case Vowels
sections.body: When ـِي ('my') attaches to a singular noun (كِتَابِي), it absorbs the short case vowel, so كِتَابِي looks identical in nominative, accusative, and genitive.
